questions.q: A force is an interaction exerted by one object on another. Which statement correctly distinguishes a contact force from a non-contact force?
options: A contact force can be exerted at a distance, while a non-contact force needs physical contact
A contact force is exerted by an object in physical contact with another object, while a non-contact force can be exerted without touching, such as gravity, magnetism and electrostatics
Contact forces are vector quantities while non-contact forces are scalar quantities
A contact force is always larger than a non-contact force
questions.explanation: A contact force is exerted by an object that is in physical contact with another (applied force, friction, normal, tension), while a non-contact force is exerted at a distance through a field — the effects of gravity, magnetism and electrostatics. Force is a vector, so both kinds have magnitude (in newtons) and direction.

questions.q: The weight of an object is given by W = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength. Which statement correctly relates mass and weight near the Earth's surface?
options: Mass is the gravitational force on an object, measured in newtons
Weight is the gravitational force on the mass, W = mg, with g about 9.8 m s⁻² at the Earth's surface, while mass is a measure of the amount of matter and remains the same wherever you are
Both the mass and the weight of an object change when it is moved to the Moon
Weight is a measure of the amount of matter in an object and is the same everywhere
questions.explanation: The weight W is the force on an object due to the pull of gravity, equal to mg, and it depends on location because g varies (about 9.8 m s⁻² on Earth, 1.6 m s⁻² on the Moon). Mass is a measure of the amount of matter and stays the same wherever you are — that is the distinction the exam tests.

questions.q: Most objects are acted upon by more than one force at a time. What is meant by the net force, Fnet, acting on an object?
options: The single largest force acting on the object
The vector sum of all the forces acting on the object
The force that the object exerts on its surroundings
The difference between the object's weight and its mass
questions.explanation: The net force is the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object. It may be equal to zero (the object is in equilibrium and keeps the same state of motion) or a non-zero vector that causes a change in the object's state of motion.

questions.q: Newton's First Law of Motion states that every object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless made to change by what?
options: A contact force that physically touches it
A non-zero net force
A change in its mass
The removal of gravity acting on it
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law: every object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless made to change by a non-zero net force. When a non-zero net force acts, the object accelerates in the direction of that net force; balanced forces (net force zero) mean no change in motion.

questions.q: From memory: define the inertia of an object and state what its inertia depends on.
keyPoints: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes to its motion.
Inertia is not a force; it is a property of all objects.
The inertia of an object depends only on its mass — a large mass is harder to get moving, stop or change direction than a small mass.
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law is also called the Law of Inertia. If you recalled that inertia is the resistance to a change in motion, that it is a property (not a force), and that it depends only on mass, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: A 65 kg physics teacher, starting from rest, glides down a slide. The net force on her during the slide is a constant 350 N. Calculate her acceleration.
questions.explanation: Apply Newton's Second Law, Fnet = ma, and rearrange for acceleration: a = Fnet / m = 350 / 65 = 5.4 m s⁻². This acceleration could then be fed into the equations of uniformly accelerated motion to find, for example, the speed at the bottom of the slide.

questions.q: A car of mass 1600 kg tows a trailer of mass 400 kg by a rigid coupling. The driving force on the car, starting from rest, is 5400 N east, and friction is ignored. Calculate the acceleration of the car and trailer.
questions.given: car \(= 1600\,\mathrm{kg}\),  trailer \(= 400\,\mathrm{kg}\),  driving force \(= 5400\,\mathrm{N}\) east,  friction ignored
working: Because the coupling is rigid, the car and trailer have equal accelerations; apply Newton's Second Law to the whole system.
questions.explanation: Treat the car and trailer as a single system of mass 2000 kg, since the rigid coupling gives them equal accelerations. The only external horizontal force is the 5400 N driving force, so a = Fnet / m = 5400 / 2000 = 2.7 m s⁻² east.

questions.q: Newton's Third Law states that whenever an object applies a force (an action) to a second object, the second applies an equal and opposite force (a reaction). Why is it incorrect to say that an action–reaction pair 'cancels out'?
options: Because one of the two forces is always larger than the other
Because the forces that make up an action–reaction pair act on different objects, so it makes no sense to add them together so they cancel out
Because reaction forces are imaginary and have no real effect
Because the action and the reaction forces act at different times
questions.explanation: The two forces in an action–reaction pair act on different objects, so they can never cancel on a single object. The motion of each object is determined by the net force acting on it. This is why, when you walk, your feet push back on the ground and the ground pushes forward on you — that forward reaction force accelerates you.

questions.q: Experiments on Newton's Second Law show how the acceleration of an object depends on the net force applied and on the mass. Which relationship is correct?
options: Acceleration is inversely proportional to the net force and proportional to the mass
Acceleration is proportional to the net force applied and inversely proportional to the mass
Acceleration is proportional to both the net force and the mass
Acceleration is independent of the net force, depending only on the mass
questions.explanation: The acceleration a of an object is proportional to the net force Fnet applied to it and inversely proportional to the mass m. Combining these gives Fnet = ma, with the constant of proportionality equal to 1 by the definition of the newton (a 1 N net force gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²).

questions.q: Distinguish between the mass and the weight of an object. (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, a scalar quantity measured in kilograms, and it is constant regardless of location. Weight is the gravitational force acting on the object, a vector quantity measured in newtons, equal to the mass times the gravitational field strength (W = mg), and it depends on the local value of g, so it changes with location.

criteria.descriptor: Defines mass as the scalar amount of matter in kilograms, constant everywhere.
Defines weight as the gravitational force in newtons, equal to mg, which varies with location.

questions.explanation: The trap is saying weight is 'how heavy something is' — that is vague. Name it as a force equal to mg, and contrast it with mass as the location-independent amount of matter.

questions.q: From memory: state the memory hook for Newton's three laws used in the episode, and describe the 'signature move' that links Dynamics back to Kinematics.
keyPoints: The hook is 'I, F, A': Inertia (first law), F = ma (second law), Action–reaction (third law).
Signature move: use the second law to find the acceleration from the net force (a = Fnet / m).
Then feed that acceleration into the suvat equations of motion to predict displacement and velocity — force to acceleration to motion.
questions.explanation: This ties the whole module together: compute the net force, divide by mass for the acceleration (Dynamics), then hand the acceleration to the equations of uniformly accelerated motion (Kinematics). If you recalled I-F-A and the two-step chain, grade Good or Easy.
